{
  "measurements": [
    {
      "statistic": "restoration of function",
      "value": 100,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the degree of restoration of rod and cone-mediated electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes in treated dog eyes compared to normal dogs.",
      "compared": "dog RPE65 gene therapy vs normal dog ERG amplitudes",
      "species": [
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "The ERG tracings show that there is excellent restoration of both rod- and cone-mediated ERG responses. The magnitude of ERG amplitudes approaches those of normal dogs."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "rescue achieved",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the degree of functional rescue achieved in human patients compared to that achieved in preclinical dog trials.",
      "compared": "human RPE65 gene therapy vs dog RPE65 gene therapy",
      "species": [
        "human",
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Despite the safe and encouraging improvement in visual function, the degree of rescue achieved in human patients has been nowhere near that achieved in the preclinical Rpe65- mutant dog trials."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "visual function improvement",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the improvement in visual function in human patients treated with RPE65 gene therapy.",
      "compared": "human RPE65 gene therapy vs baseline",
      "species": [
        "human"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "The results have been very encouraging, with patients having improved ability to perceive light, improved visual acuity in some instances, improved pupillary responses and visual cortex responses, and for some patients improved ability to negotiate obstacles."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "ERG responses",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the change in electroretinogram (ERG) responses in human patients treated with RPE65 gene therapy.",
      "compared": "human RPE65 gene therapy vs baseline",
      "species": [
        "human"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "With the exception of one patient with a transient improvement in the multifocal ERG, there was no change in ERG responses."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "ERG improvement",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the improvement in electroretinogram (ERG) responses in dogs treated with RPE65 gene therapy.",
      "compared": "dog RPE65 gene therapy vs baseline",
      "species": [
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "In contrast, in dogs there is a remarkable improvement in the ERG, indicating restoration of function close to normal levels (Fig. 1)."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "vision after treatment",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the level of vision in dogs after RPE65 gene therapy treatment.",
      "compared": "dog RPE65 gene therapy vs normal",
      "species": [
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Vision in dogs after treatment appears very close to normal, while human patients remain visually impaired."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "photoreceptor number decline",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the rate of photoreceptor number decline in human patients compared to dogs.",
      "compared": "human vs dog photoreceptor number decline",
      "species": [
        "human",
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "One major reason is that human patients have a much faster relative decline in photoreceptor numbers compared with dogs and invariably already have a marked loss of photoreceptors when treated, whereas the dogs treated up to middle age have good preservation of photoreceptors that respond well to restoration of visual cycle function."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "rod-mediated ERG responses",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the improvement in rod-mediated electroretinogram (ERG) responses in treated dog eyes compared to untreated eyes.",
      "compared": "Pde6b mutant dog gene therapy vs untreated eye",
      "species": [
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": 8,
      "n_counts": "dogs",
      "verbatim": "The treated eyes were reported to have improved rod-mediated ERGs, and dim light vision testing of each eye in turn showed that when the treated eye was uncovered the dogs were able to negotiate obstacles, but when the untreated eye was uncovered they acted as if they were blind."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "cone ERG responses",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the restoration of cone electroretinogram (ERG) responses in treated dog eyes.",
      "compared": "Rpgrip1-deficient dog gene therapy vs baseline",
      "species": [
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": 7,
      "n_counts": "dogs",
      "verbatim": "There was restoration of cone ERG responses in the treated eyes and a partial preservation of rod electroretinographic responses."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "daytime vision",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the improvement in daytime vision in treated dogs with achromatopsia.",
      "compared": "achromatopsia dog gene therapy vs baseline",
      "species": [
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "A dog with successful treatment had restored daytime vision as assessed by ability to negotiate a maze and cone function was recordable by the ERG."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "cone function",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the recordable cone function in dogs treated for achromatopsia.",
      "compared": "achromatopsia dog gene therapy vs baseline",
      "species": [
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "A dog with successful treatment had restored daytime vision as assessed by ability to negotiate a maze and cone function was recordable by the ERG."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "reversal of lesions",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the reversal of retinal lesions in dogs treated for canine multifocal retinopathy.",
      "compared": "cmr-affected dog gene therapy vs baseline",
      "species": [
        "dog"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "The therapy was reported to reverse lesions and to have no adverse effects."
    }
  ],
  "headline_index": 2,
  "what_the_study_did": "This review summarizes spontaneous canine models for inherited retinal dystrophies and their use in translational gene therapy trials, comparing outcomes in human clinical trials with preclinical dog trials.",
  "what_it_found": "Dog models have been critical in advancing gene therapy for inherited retinal diseases to clinical trials, showing promise but also highlighting species-specific differences in outcomes.",
  "key_quotes": [
    {
      "quote": "Despite the safe and encouraging improvement in visual function, the degree of rescue achieved in human patients has been nowhere near that achieved in the preclinical Rpe65- mutant dog trials.",
      "topic": "Human vs Dog Rescue"
    },
    {
      "quote": "In contrast, in dogs there is a remarkable improvement in the ERG, indicating restoration of function close to normal levels (Fig. 1).",
      "topic": "Dog ERG Improvement"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Vision in dogs after treatment appears very close to normal, while human patients remain visually impaired.",
      "topic": "Dog vs Human Vision"
    },
    {
      "quote": "One major reason is that human patients have a much faster relative decline in photoreceptor numbers compared with dogs and invariably already have a marked loss of photoreceptors when treated, whereas the dogs treated up to middle age have good preservation of photoreceptors that respond well to restoration of visual cycle function.",
      "topic": "Photoreceptor Loss Rate"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Preclinical studies in dogs have been critical in bringing gene therapy to treat inherited retinal disease to the clinic.",
      "topic": "Dog Model Importance"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Species differences do exist, meaning that extrapolation of successes between mouse, dog, and human should not be assumed.",
      "topic": "Species Differences"
    }
  ]
}
